div.head:
TO
THE RIGHT HONORABLE

GEORGE HENRY ROSE, M.P.
&c. &c.
div.p:
Sir,
The language of dedication is so frequently that of flattery, and falttery is so contemptible in your eyes, that I prefer the risk of appearing ungrateful, to the chance of being deemed in the smallest degree sycophantic.

Therefore I avoid all the usual expressions of praise of thankfulness, and merely state, that during my residence in your family, great and uniform as was your personal kindness, my highest gratification consisted in remarkiing the preference which you gave to the discharge of religious duties above all others, and in
witnessing your efforts in teaching the ignorant and converting the sceptical. It was not more delightful to me than beneficial, that I should be permitted to participate with you in such employments; and I shall ever consider the period of my Chaplaincy to the British Embassy at Berlin, as fraught with great improvement to myself in all that regards my office.

During the remainder of a life, which must be devoted to unremitting labour, and therefore cannot pass without a large portion of anxiety, I shall never cease to derive comfort from the recollection of my having lived on terms of amity and intimacy with one, who regards as nothing the distinctions of rank, the applause of man, and the favour of princes, when compared with the testimony of his own conscience, in a diligent search into the hid treasures of the Gosepl.

Such being the sentiments, Sir, you will not doubt that I duly value your permission of dedicating the following Discourses to you; and that, in so doing, I do not inscribe them to the Senator, the Privy Counsellor, nor to the
Minister, but to the enlightened and strenuous chamption of our Church—to one who is in truth, and in deed, a Christian.

I have the honour to be,
SIR,
With the greatest respect,
Your most obedient,
And very humble Servant,
HENRY THOMAS AUSTEN.
